items.title: Arrested generals and a threatened VP: President's son fuels Ugandan succession fever
items.summary: The 52-year-old general’s provocative posts and military threats have fuelled rumours of a dynastic succession.
items.content:
In Uganda's military, even senior generals are finding that their rank offers little protection from the wrath of the country's powerful army chief.

Over the past 15 months, at least a dozen generals and senior officers have been arrested under Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is also the son of President Yoweri Museveni, in a crackdown that has unsettled the military's top ranks.

The arrests come amid growing political tensions over who will succeed Museveni, who has ruled Uganda for four decades.

Gen Kainerugaba, 52, is widely seen as a potential successor, although his ambitions appear to be facing resistance within the ruling party.

This week, he threatened Vice-President Jessica Alupo with dismissal and possible arrest, while suggesting he should take her position.

The ruling National Resistance Movement (NRM) has, however, rejected reports that its senior leadership had rejected a proposal to back Gen Kainerugaba as the next president, describing the claims as "completely false".

This has all fuelled speculation that the arrests are part of an effort to sideline military officers opposed to the general's presidential ambitions.

Others see the arrests as evidence of an anti-corruption drive in which senior commanders are held to account.

At the centre of the tension are two powerful powerful institutions: the military, where Gen Kainerugaba wields considerable influence, and the NRM, where questions about his political ambitions appear to be dividing senior figures.

A recent meeting of NRM's top leadership ended without agreement on a proposal to position Gen Kainerugaba as Museveni's successor, according to the AFP news agency.

Five party sources who attended the closed-door meeting told AFP that a vote was abandoned after several members spoke against the proposal.

Uganda's news website ChimpReports, however, said that most members who spoke backed the general's potential presidency, although some questioned his readiness for civilian leadership.

In a statement on Thursday, NRM Secretary General Richard Todwong Awany confirmed that the party had met on 10 November to discuss "political, social and economic issues".

He dismissed reports that the meeting had rejected a proposal to position Gen Kainerugaba as Uganda's next president, saying the party would communicate any decisions "through the right channel, at the right time".

Dr Gerald Bareebe, a Ugandan-born political scientist at Canada's York University, sees a connection between the arrests and political manoeuvring over Museveni's succession, often referred to as the "Muhoozi Project".

"Senior officers believed not to support the project have been arrested, detained or charged with corruption and treason," he tells the BBC.

He says the allegations against some officers were widely viewed as politically motivated, reflecting growing divisions within the military over the succession question.

Some of those detained have since been released, apparently after securing the general's forgiveness.

The detention of one of the country's most prominent former commanders, Lt Gen Peter Elwelu , has brought the crackdown into sharper focus.

The former deputy army chief was detained on 2 November over allegations that he had plotted to destabilise the eastern Teso region.

His fall from grace followed a series of social media posts by Kainerugaba, who accused him of treachery and announced that he had been stripped of his three-star rank and demoted.

"The traitor Peter Elwelu is hereby stripped of his ranks. He is demoted to Private," Kainerugaba wrote on X.

He also claimed that more than 20 soldiers linked to Elwelu had been arrested.

The announcement raised legal questions, with Ugandan media reporting that military regulations do not allow a senior officer to be stripped of his rank through a social media post.

The army later confirmed Elwelu's detention, saying they had recovered 15 guns, military uniforms and two pickup trucks linked to him. His family has rejected the allegations.

Elwelu is among at least a dozen generals and senior officers detained since April 2025, according to an investigation by Uganda's Daily Monitor newspaper.

They include three former military intelligence chiefs who once oversaw some of Uganda's most sensitive security operations.

This army chief threatened to castrate opposition leader and claimed descent from Jesus

The 'shadow army' helping Uganda's long-serving president keep an iron grip on power

Maj Gen James Birungi, a former head of defence intelligence and security, was arrested in August 2025, on allegations including treason, terrorism and corruption.

He was charged before a military court but later released after Gen Kainerugaba announced that he had "forgiven" him.

Another former intelligence chief, Maj Gen Abel Kandiho, was detained in September this year over allegations of providing false intelligence and treachery. He remains in detention, according to the Daily Monitor.

His predecessor, Brig-Gen Charles Bakahumura, was also arrested in September over similar allegations, but was later released after the army chief announced that he had forgiven him.

Other officers have faced accusations ranging from stealing military fuel to taking money to spy on military communications.

The military has defended the arrests as part of efforts to tackle corruption and criminality within the armed forces.

Ugandan security analyst Freddie David Egesa says the arrests reflect investigations involving different security agencies, rather than an army-led purge.

He argues that detaining senior officers helps protect witnesses and demonstrates the seriousness of the anti-corruption drive.

"Gen Muhoozi has the overall duty to permit the investigation team to arrest these high-profile people, in consultation with the commander-in-chief," Egesa says, adding: "The arrests are not summarily done."

But Bareebe sees a wider political motive, arguing that officers suspected of opposing to Gen Kainerugaba's presidential ambitions are being targeted.

"The result is a broad purge that has affected both serving and retired officers perceived to be anti-Muhoozi," he says.

He points to divisions between the elite Special Forces Command (SFC), which he says is largely loyal to the president's son, and army commanders who remain unconvinced about his succession.

The allegations against the officers are at different stages, with some facing charges, others in detention without publicly announced charges, and several having been released.

Bareebe also questions whether military trials can deliver independent proceedings.

"Many Ugandans regard the charges as politically motivated and therefore expect little justice," he adds.

He alleges that some officers have had charges dropped after closed-door negotiations with the president and his son, during which they were pressured to declare support for Gen Kainerugaba.

Government spokesperson Allan Kasujja dismissed the claims of a succession fallout as "hogwash".

Unlike his predecessors, who communicated through official military channels, Gen Kainerugaba frequently uses X to announce arrests, criticise public officials and comment on domestic and international affairs. Some have sparked diplomatic controversy.

On the night of 9 November, he turned his attention to Vice-President Jessica Alupo, demanding to take her job.

"Whoever is in that office should prepare to hand it over soon," he wrote, in posts that he later deleted.

He also questioned Alupo's loyalty and threatened her dismissal, adding that the government would operate "on military terms", if he became his father's deputy.

The following day, his X account, which had nearly 1.4 million followers, became inaccessible.

It was unclear whether he deactivated it himself, which he has done before, or the platform had suspended it.

Egesa says Gen Kainerugaba's controversial posts reflect his preferred style of communicating, but adds that security analysts are assessing their implications for Uganda's political and military stability.

Bareebe, however, sees them as part of a broader effort by the army chief to extend his influence into civilian politics.

He says the public confrontation with senior political figures illustrates how the succession debate was spilling beyond the army and into the ruling party.

Gen Kainerugaba was appointed army chief in March 2024, after previously commanding the SFC, which is responsible for protecting the president and strategic installations.

Under Uganda's military structure, he reports directly to Museveni, giving him considerable influence over the army.

Bareebe argues that the SFC's loyalty to the president and his son could prove crucial in any future transfer of power.

"The regular army remains important but has been sidelined by the SFC, which now functions as a personal army for Museveni and his son," he adds.

At the heart of the tension is the question of who will succeed Museveni, 82, who has ruled Uganda since 1986, when his rebel National Resistance Army seized power after a five-year guerrilla war.

items.title: Setback for SpaceX Starship rocket's double-catch test
items.summary: Elon Musk’s company aborted an attempted catch of the rocket’s booster - instead it came down in the ocean.
items.content:
SpaceX has aborted its attempt to catch the bottom part of its huge Starship rocket during its latest test flight.

The company had aimed to catch it using the mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - on the launch tower as it returned to Earth, but instead it was diverted to the ocean, bursting into flames as it came down.

The top part of the rocket is now continuing its journey to space and SpaceX will decide whether it will try to catch this rocket stage at about 15:15 local time (21:15 GMT) on Saturday.

It is the aerospace firm's first attempt to fully recover its rocket, paving the way for making Starship fully reusable so it can fly repeatedly and reduce costs.

The 124m-tall (407ft) rocket successfully blasted off from the Starbase launchpad in Boca Chica, Texas at 16:45 local time on Friday.

The launch tower there was supposed to catch the bottom part of the rocket - the Super Heavy booster - six-and-a-half minutes later when it returned, but it was instead diverted to the ocean.

During a livestream of the launch, a SpaceX spokesperson said: "Safety is always the number one priority and we're still testing out things that we haven't done before on these vehicles, and so we are prioritising making sure that we can perform each manoeuvre safely."

The top part of the rocket, called the Ship, is continuing its journey to space, where it is deploying 26 satellites. These will form part of the Starlink constellation that provides high-speed internet.

The Ship is due to complete 14 orbits around the Earth before returning to the launch tower 22.5 hours after taking off, where a second catch may be attempted.

SpaceX has managed to catch the Super Heavy Booster on three earlier test flights.

But the upper stage of the rocket, which only reached orbit for the first time in September, has never been grabbed by the chopsticks.

Before the flight, SpaceX said it would only decide to try to catch the Ship after carefully assessing the vehicle while it was in space.

If any problems are detected, there are various points during the flight when the rocket stage can be brought down in the ocean.

Building a fully reusable rocket is a long-held ambition for SpaceX.

In 2015, it became the first company to vertically land part of a rocket with its Falcon 9 booster.

Falcon 9 rockets now fly more than 100 times a year and the ability to reuse the bottom part of the rocket has dramatically cut the costs of launch.

But landing an entire Starship rocket could take this to the next level, says Prof Malcolm Macdonald, president of Royal Aeronautical Society.

"Full reusability has the potential to fundamentally change the economics of accessing space," he said.

"One successful flight will not prove that model, but it could mark an important transition: from demonstrating that Starship can fly, to demonstrating how Starship could operate."

After SpaceX became a public company earlier this year, its shareholders will be carefully monitoring this flight, as will Nasa.

The progress of Starship has direct implications for Nasa's attempt to land humans on the Moon in 2028 - a highly ambitious timeline.

Watch: From launch to fiery splashdown, SpaceX's Starship completes orbit test

SpaceX has been given a Nasa contract to configure the Ship into a lander that will eventually take astronauts down to the lunar surface.

But it is not the only company working with Nasa. Blue Origin, owned by rival tech billionaire Jeff Bezos, also has a contract to use its New Glenn rocket and lander for the Moon touchdown.

Both companies will also play a key role in the Artemis III mission, which is currently planned for summer 2027 - another challenging schedule.

Four astronauts in Nasa's Orion spacecraft will attempt to dock with both SpaceX and Blue Origin's landers during the voyage.

Starship will need to make a lot of progress in the coming months to meet these commitments - the pace of the rocket's development has been far slower than SpaceX had intended.

But Blue Origin also has much work to do. The company suffered a major setback earlier this year when its rocket exploded, totally destroying its launchpad in Florida.

Blue Origin had said its spacecraft would be back in action by the end of this year, but a return to flight has now been delayed to early in 2027.

Nasa is under pressure to meet its timelines. Its administrator Jared Isaacman has said the US was in a race with China to get to the Moon. China plans to land its Taikonauts on the lunar surface by 2030.

items.title: What happened to 3Com?
items.summary: Article URL: https://dfarq.homeip.net/what-happened-to-3com/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50491830 Points: 133 # Comments: 67
items.content:
3Com was a high flying maker of network cards and other network equipment. And then they disappeared with a whimper on November 11, 2009. What happened to 3Com?

Around the time of the dotcom boom , 3Com was a 5.8 billion dollar company. They were founded in 1979 by Bob Metcalfe, the co-inventor of Ethernet. And for the next two decades, they were the go-to brand for network cards. While the 3C501 network card is notoriously bad, their other cards from the 1980s and 1990s are very well regarded, and always were.

They cost more, but had good driver support, the hardware worked reliably, and they were a known quantity. And 3Com made them in the United States, which was becoming unusual even in the 1990s.

I once worked in a shop that didn’t allow network equipment unless it was one of three brands. 3Com was one of them, along with Cisco and Intel. If you plugged a no name NE2000 clone card into the network and had problems, the IT department would replace the card and bill your department. There was a saying in the 1980s that no one got fired for buying IBM. When it came to networking, one could say the same for 3Com, during their prime.

And they were huge. In 1995, 3Com bought the naming rights to Candlestick Park, the legendary baseball/football stadium in San Francisco. It held those rights until 2002.

But after the dotcom bust, 3Com faded away. What happened to 3Com, ultimately, was a series of bad decisions that led to a loss of profitability. Some of them may have made sense at the time. But not all of them.

The first thing that happened was 3Com walked away from its enterprise networking equipment business. Admittedly Cisco was hard to compete with. But 3Com was the only brand succeeding at doing it. The logic behind the move always puzzled analysts, because it didn’t save any money. Revenue dropped, and 3Com angered its customers and dealers. It’s likely many started buying Intel cards afterward, since they had to change vendors anyway.

Many corporations like to buy multiple things from a single supplier. This was one reason IBM stayed in the PC business for several years into the 21st century even though they were losing money on it. The computers weren’t profitable, but they made it easier to sell services, and the services were profitable. There is always the fear that two vendors will point fingers at each other, saying the network problem was caused by the hub and the network card being mismatched brands. Interoperability was the whole idea behind Ethernet, but not everyone understood that. One could commend 3Com for not wanting to exploit that misunderstanding. But it came at a financial cost.

It also didn’t help that the company branched into other businesses outside its core. The purchase of US Robotics was a key example. US Robotics made modems and Palm Pilots . For a short time, that was big business. But 3Com paid a premium price for products with a limited shelf life left in them.

Nothing good happened to 3Com after that. It took 3 years for Cisco to go from being 90% the size of 3Com to double the size of 3Com. The profitability of selling network adapters dropped. And by the time 3Com realized they needed to get back into network equipment, it was an expensive proposition. From 2000 to 2005, the company didn’t turn a profit.

Ultimately, 3Com failed because it was too dependent on network cards. Network cards accounted for about half their revenue during their bust years. And their cards were expensive. Intel undercut their price to try to gain market share, and they succeeded.

And then they did exactly the wrong thing. It was the late ’90s, and they bought their way into the modem business. The dial-up modem business. At that point in time, everyone knew broadband was the future, they just didn’t know exactly when it was going to arrive. Yet 3Com had no plan to get into that business. It was like betting on AOL even though they were in the position to know the future belonged to AT&T .

Making matters worse, minimum viable product-style modems undercut US Robotics modems, just like the network card business. Not that Intel cards were a minimum viable product. But pretty much any ’90s network card not made by Intel or 3Com was.

3Com sought partnerships, most notably a partnership with Chinese networking giant Huawei. There were even rumors of Huawei buying 3com, though that deal never went through. And 3Com started making product overseas as a cost reducing measure. But ultimately, nothing could make up for all that lost time and all those bad decisions.

So what happened to 3Com? 3Com didn’t go out of business and they didn’t sell out to Huawei. They got Compaqed . Hewlett-Packard bought them out, which seems to be where every great ’90s technology company went to die. Hewlett-Packard paid 2.7 billion dollars in late 2009 for 3Com’s assets.

HP still sells network equipment like switches, routers, and access points. But they’re not as big of a name in networking as 3Com had been. And the 3Com pedigree isn’t the selling point. If they put a brand on it other than HP, it’s the newer Aruba brand, not 3Com. The selling point is the price being lower than Cisco. This makes them attractive to executives or purchasing agents looking to cut costs, consolidate vendors, or both. HP will usually beat Cisco’s price. And if the IT department is under pressure to reduce the number of vendors it buys from, HP sells more things than Cisco. So HP gets in the door for one of those reasons, and when their network equipment turns out to be no worse than Cisco equipment, they stay with it. At least until Dell comes around offering discounts.

But the network cards are long gone. When you buy an HP branded network card today, guess what it is? It’s an Intel card with HP’s logo engraved on it. Unless HP is trying to control costs, in which case it just has a sticker.

Vintage 3Com network cards are very popular with retro computing enthusiasts. It had top-tier name recognition in the 80s and 90s. All but their very earliest cards generally have good driver support, work well, and are easier to configure than most of the cheaper competitors.

My favorite retro network card is a very specific Intel card , but if you need a card for anything from the 286 to the Pentium II era, you can do far worse than a 3com 3c509 ISA card or 3c905 PCI card. It’s absolutely period correct and absolutely something a knowledgeable professional would have used at the time. I have better luck with the ISA cards under DOS than the PCI cards, so if I want to run DOS and do any networking, I use a 3c509 ISA card in the system. But for Windows 95 and newer, the 3c905 PCI card works really well and is very cheap and common.

David Farquhar is a computer security professional, entrepreneur, and author. He has written professionally about computers since 1991, so he was writing about retro computers when they were still new. He has been working in IT professionally since 1994 and has specialized in vulnerability management since 2013. He holds Security+ and CISSP certifications. Today he blogs five times a week, mostly about retro computers and retro gaming covering the time period from 1975 to 2000.

items.title: 'Miracle on Mississippi' - All passengers rescued after New Orleans cruise ship collision
items.summary: The collision leaves 32 people in hospital with non-critical injuries, but no-one unaccounted for.
items.content:
Some 130 people on a cruise ship docked in New Orleans have been rescued after it was struck by a tanker.

The cruise ship, American Heritage, was left lying on its side in the Mississippi River after it was hit by the cargo vessel Atlantic Asphalt.

The collision left 32 people from the stricken riverboat in hospital with non-critical injuries, but no-one unaccounted for. Officials hailed it as a "miracle on the Mississippi".

The exact cause of the crash remains under investigation, but US Coast Guard Capt Melanie Burnham said: "There seems to be some type of a loss of steering."

New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno told a news conference that all credit in the rescue effort should go to first responders who "literally jumped right in to help".

"We have zero people unaccounted for, which truly is a miracle on the Mississippi," Moreno said.

Calls about the collision began around 13:30 EST (18:30 GMT) on Friday, when people began trying to help passengers escape the boat as it took on water, Port of New Orleans chief Melanie Montroll told the news conference.

There were about 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, on the American Heritage at the time of the collision, according to the port authority.

Passengers began getting off the paddlewheeler vessel, operated by American Cruise Lines, as it started listing before tipping onto its side, Moreno said.

Tugboat operators, police and other rescuers rushed to help while officials shut down traffic in the Mississippi River during the rescue effort.

The American Heritage had been finishing an eight-day cruise calling at destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi along the waterway.

US President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social that the rescue had been an "incredible job".

Governor Jeff Landry also hailed the rescue as a "miracle on the Mississippi" given the "sheer number of people who were on that cruise ship" who were rescued.

Ships have operated safely on the Mississippi River for years, Landry said, pledging to investigate what had occurred.

Jamie Holford, a witness to the crash, told the BBC's US partner CBS that he had seen the cruise ship hit the dock following the collision.

"It sounded like a war movie. Just imagine tons of steel crunching. That's what it sounded like," he said. "It looked like something off the Titanic."

Holford added that he had seen passengers and crew "hollering" and "crying" as they tried to get off the ship while it was sinking.

The American Heritage can carry up to 150 guests and features a glass-enclosed restaurant, fitness centre and three guest lounges, according to its website.

items.title: Usa, router in tilt per sovraccarico dati, stop ai voli per 4 ore. “Colpa dei sistemi obsoleti”
items.summary: “Non è stato un attacco hacker”, ha precisato il segretario ai Trasporti Sean Duffy. Cbs, blocco aereo causato da aggiornamento software
items.content:
Venerdì di caos per oltre un milione e mezzo di viaggiatori intrappolati negli aeroporti Usa. Uno stop a livello nazionale ha bloccato il traffico aereo del Paese per più di quattro ore. A disporlo è stata l'autorità americana dell'aviazione per "circostanze straordinarie e motivi di sicurezza ". Un probabile sovraccarico dei dati trasmessi dai router avrebbe mandato fuori uso molte frequenze radio utilizzate per comunicare con i piloti a terra. Il segretario alla Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin , che ha parlato con i giornalisti alla Casa Bianca, ha frenato il panico: "Non è un altro 11 settembre", e ha spiegato che non ci sono collegamenti con il blocco delle mail e dei servizi Microsoft delle ultime 48 ore. Non succedeva dal 2023, quando l’autorità americana dell’aviazione fermò i voli nazionali per un problema tecnico nel sistema di allerta per i piloti. Prima ancora avvenne l’ 11 settembre 2001 , dopo l’attentato alle Torri Gemelle.

Aeroporti di Roma: “Operativi voli in partenza per gli Usa ma inevitabili ritardi”

Media Usa: “Serviranno giorni per riportare il traffico aereo alla normalità”

Potrebbero volerci giorni affinché il traffico aereo Usa torni alla normalità dopo il blocco dei voli della scorsa notte. E' quanto affermano dai media statunitensi. Con così tanti aerei impossibilitati a decollare, scrive la Cnn, gli aeroporti hanno esaurito i gate e lo spazio sulle piste per parcheggiare i velivoli. Alcuni voli sono ripresi, ma enormi folle rimangono bloccate negli aeroporti di tutti gli Stati Uniti, mentre le autorità avvertono che ci vorrà del tempo per smaltire l'arretrato. Secondo Vikrant Vaze, docente al Dartmouth College ed esperto di logistica nell'aviazione commerciale, sentito dal New York Times, sarà necessaria una notevole dose di "acrobazie logistiche" per riportare velivoli, passeggeri ed equipaggi di ogni compagnia aerea nelle posizioni corrette, ha spiegato. Le compagnie aeree possono adottare alcune misure di emergenza per ripristinare la regolarità delle operazioni, come l'impiego di equipaggi di riserva o il trasferimento di aerei vuoti verso altre destinazioni. Secondo Vaze, un elemento favorevole è la disponibilità delle ore notturne - quando solitamente si registra un minor numero di voli nazionali - che consente di smaltire parte degli arretrati accumulati.

Ci sarebbe l'aggiornamento di un software dietro al collasso delle comunicazioni che ha portato al blocco del traffico aereo per quasi cinque ore negli Stati Uniti. A sostenerlo è la Cbs. "Un aggiornamento della rete di comunicazione privata che collega il sistema di controllo del traffico aereo americano ha causato il riavvio del sistema che è andato in blocco", ha spiegato la rete televisiva. Da qui è derivata l'interruzione delle comunicazioni. Il sistema è gestito da L3Harris, che non ha risposto immediatamente alla richiesta di commento di Cbs. L3Harris Technologies è una grande azienda della difesa statunitense, quotata alla Borsa di New York, con sede a Melbourne, in Florida. Ha un fatturato annuo superiore a 21,9 miliardi di dollari e attività in oltre 100 Paesi. I suoi clienti principali sono i dipartimenti e le agenzie del governo statunitense, a partire dal Pentagono.

Aeroporti di Roma: “Operativi voli in partenza per gli Usa ma inevitabili ritardi”

All'aeroporto di Roma Fiumicino risultano operativi i voli in partenza per gli Usa dopo la revoca del blocco da parte della Federal Aviation Administration (Faa), l'authority di controllo aereo. Al momento, in mattinata, secondo quanto visualizzabile dai monitor aeroportuali, alcuni collegamenti accusano degli inevitabili ritardi, alla luce del blocco dei voli Usa di ieri sera: è il caso di quelli diretti a Chicago (United) con oltre due ore, Atlanta (Delta) di un'ora e mezza, Detroit (Delta) di 30 minuti e due per New York (Delta) rispettivamente di poco meno di 2 ore e 30 minuti. Sul fronte degli arrivi, risulta cancellato in mattinata un volo da Dallas (American Airlines) mentre altri voli, da New York, Atlanta, Filadelfia, Detroit sono in arrivo con ritardi compresi fra i 30 minuti e le 2 ore. Più pesanti i ritardi per altri voli in arrivo, previsti nel pomeriggio, da Los Angeles, Houston, Atlanta, compresi fra le 3 e le 4 ore. E' quanto fanno sapere da Aeroporti di Roma.

Usa: oltre 15mila i voli cancellati o rinviati, altri 3mila oggi

Negli Usa migliaia di passeggeri stanno trascorrendo una notte incerta, dormendo sui pavimenti degli aeroporti o bloccati in code estenuanti nelle prime ore di sabato. Venerdì, secondo la Cnn, sono stati oltre 15mila i voli negli Stati Uniti che hanno subito ritardi o cancellazioni, e si prevede che circa 3.000 voli subiranno la stessa sorte nella giornata di sabato.

Trump al Senato: “Ora trenta miliardi per i sistemi di controllo dei voli”

Dopo il blackout di 4 ore al traffico aereo negli Stati Uniti, il presidente Donald Trump è in pressing sul Senato affinché approvi il pacchetto da 30 miliardi per l'ammodernamento dei sistemi di controllo dei voli. Secondo la Cnn, Trump ha sentito il senatore Eric Schmitt che aveva presentato a settembre il Modern Skies Act con la richiesta di fondi. Proprio ieri mattina, l'amministrazione aveva inviato una lettera ai leader del Senato per sollecitare l'approvazione del provvedimento. La missiva aveva la firma del direttore dell'Ufficio Bilancio, Russ Vought, e del segretario ai trasporti Sean Duffy.

Sono stati più di 7.700 i voli cancellati nelle scorse ore da e per gli Stati Uniti ai quali si sommano altri 2.000 che saranno annullati nelle prossime ore. Lo riferisce la Cnn, citando dati di FlightAware, secondo cui sono stati oltre 8.000 i voli con ritardi mentre per oggi più di 300 subiranno variazioni di orario.

Sono stati più di 7.700 i voli cancellati ieri negli Stati Uniti per lo stop di quattro ore al traffico aereo e oltre 8.000 quelli ritardati. Lo riferisce la Cnn citando il sito FlightAware. I disagi continueranno anche oggi, con più di 2.000 voli già annullati.

Duffy, 'non so dire se si verificherà lo stesso scenario di problemi tlc'

"Accadrà di nuovo esattamente la stessa cosa? Non so, non so dire se si verificherà proprio questo scenario". Lo ha detto il segretario ai Trasporti Sean Duffy, nel corso del briefing sul blocco dei voli a livello nazionale per i problemi alla sicurezza legati alle comunicazioni. I nuovi aggiornamenti tecnologici hanno sovraccaricato il sistema preesistente di controllo in capo alla Federal Aviation Administration, ormai obsoleto, mettendo in crisi le apparecchiature in uso. "Continuerà a guastarsi", ha detto Duffy, riferendosi alla tecnologia che la Faa stava cercando di aggiornare e di modernizzare.

"Abbiamo identificato il problema. I nostri centri e i nostri tracon sono operativi. Alle 8:15 di stasera, ora della costa orientale, abbiamo riaperto lo spazio aereo". Lo annuncia il segretario di Stato ai Trasporti, Sean Duffy, nel corso di una cinferenza stampa alla Casa bianca. "Ora, questo significa che tutti i voli voleranno correttamente? Se siete in un aeroporto, controllate con la vostra compagnia aerea, dipende se abbiamo equipaggi disponibili", dice ai viaggiatori in attesa. "Abbiamo piloti e assistenti di volo disponibili per far volare il vostro volo, cercheremo di spostarne il più possibile stasera. In caso contrario, inizieremo domani mattina. Ma ci vorrà del tempo per annullare quello che è successo questo pomeriggio".

Mullin: “Nessun collegamento tra il blocco dei voli e Microsoft”

"Voglio assicurarmi che tutti capiscano che non c'è alcun collegamento" tra il blocco dei voli nel cieli degli Usa e Microsoft. "So che molte persone stanno facendo questo collegamento. Per quanto ne sappiamo finora, non c'è stato alcun attacco informatico. Stiamo ancora lavorando su questo processo, i nostri team stanno lavorando". Così il segretario della Sicurezza interna degli Stati Uniti, Markwayne Mullin, nel corso di una conferenza stampa alla Casa bianca. "Siamo strutturati per gestire crisi come questa. Ed è esattamente quello che stiamo facendo", sottolinea Mullin.

Il segretario ai trasporti chiede al Congresso 50 miliardi, 'blocco voli per infrastrutture tlc obsolete'

Il segretario ai trasporti Usa, Sean Duffy, ha imputato a "switch e router davvero intasati di dati" il blocco dei voli negli Usa su scala nazionale. Duffy, in un briefing alla Casa Bianca, ha citato "decine di migliaia di passeggeri bloccati", chiedendo al Congresso 50 miliardi per migliorare le relative infrastrutture. Il segretario alla Sicurezza interna, Markwayne Mullin, ha respinto le speculazioni online sull'interruzione delle operazioni di volo, insistendo che i passeggeri non sono mai stato in pericolo. "Non c'è mai stata alcuna vita a rischio. Non c'erano voli a rischio".

Il blocco dei decolli aerei negli Stati Uniti, che ha causato la sospensione di migliaia di voli, è stato revocato

'Trump ritiene il blocco dei voli dovuto a infrastrutture obsolete'

Il presidente Trump ha riferito che il guasto ai sistemi della Federal Aviation Administration (Faa), con il blocco dei voli, non sembra essere riconducibile a un attacco informatico ("non ne è emersa alcuna traccia dopo le verifiche") o all'IA, ma a infrastrutture obsolete e malfunzionanti. Lo riporta Fox News, aggiungendo che nessuno ha rivendicato l'accaduto, cosa che solitamente avviene in caso di attacco hacker "su larga scala contro infrastrutture critiche." Trump ha spiegato che parte delle apparecchiature della Faa ha 55 anni e non è mai stata sostituita, malgrado le discussioni in merito con il Congresso.

Departures in the 30 minutes before the selected time, as a share of the same half-hour a week earlier, at the 16 largest airports. An airport counts as back once it holds three-quarters of its usual departures for two readings in a row.

Estimated commercial departures missed since 3:30 pm ET: the count for the same hours a week earlier minus this week's, from tracking data. On the right, how many left, out of the number a week earlier. Dot: departures in the last 30 minutes (red almost none, amber reduced, green near normal).

— . The feed lists only airports with a specific entry; during the nationwide stop every US airport is affected, listed or not.

items.title: After a summer win, India's Gen Z protesters face a winter of uncertainty
items.summary: A new wave of youth dissent swept India this summer, fuelled by frustration and irreverent online satire.
items.content:
Cheers erupted at Delhi's Jantar Mantar protest site in July as news broke that Gen-Z protests had forced federal education minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign.

One protester turned to me, beaming: "This is the youth's victory."

Just over three months later, the mood has shifted dramatically. Student protesters are now struggling even to assemble. Demonstrations by the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) last month over voting rights were met with sweeping restrictions and thousands of peaceful protesters were detained .

The summer had seen a new wave of dissent in India, driven by deep frustration among the youth and fuelled by irreverent online satire.

The movement spread across the country, and Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a leader with a strongman image, unaccustomed to open criticism or mockery, struggled to contain it. But the government's increasingly forceful security response suggests it has learned from its rare concession to protesters, invoking public order to curb dissent.

The ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) national spokesperson Syed Zafar Islam rejected accusations of heavy-handedness and told the BBC: "The right to protest and freedom of expression is mandated by the constitution, but it has to be done within the law. It cannot override the rights of others, at the cost of public security".

This is by no means the first time the Modi government has faced large-scale protests.

But the breadth of them pose a challenge for the BJP, according to Yamini Aiyar, former president of the Centre for Policy Research and visiting professor at Brown University.

"They are not defined by caste, gender or economic class," Aiyar said. "Even some of the core BJP base, the upwardly mobile, lower-income classes, were attracted by the movement."

The scale of the youth protests is also magnified by its online presence. Protesters have broken a longstanding political taboo, openly mocking the prime minister online.

"It's more than just laughs," said Sakhi, a student protester who identifies as they/them and affiliated with one of Delhi University's left-wing student organisations.

"The fear of repercussions in other generations isn't felt as much in ours," they said. "Comedy is a new language to challenge authority."

Previous protest movements posed serious challenges to Modi but were easier to dismiss as representing narrow sections of society or to label "anti-national", according to Aiyar.

In 2020, farmers protesting against controversial agricultural reforms were blocked from entering Delhi, leading to months of demonstrations and, at times, clashes on the capital's borders. After a year of protests, the government abandoned the reforms.

Protests against a contentious citizenship law in 2019 and 2020 are a stark reminder of the powers of the judiciary should anyone be deemed a national security threat.

Student activist Umar Khalid was arrested under anti-terror laws after violent clashes in Delhi that killed 53 people, mostly Muslims. He was accused of being a "key conspirator". He has now spent more than six years in jail without his trial having begun.

His partner Banojyotsna Lahiri told the BBC they have no regrets, but that the situation instilled "a kind of fear that has prevailed".

"We are just looking at a very dark mesh of empty space, because we don't know when the endpoint is," Lahiri said. Khalid's latest appeal was lodged this month.

Aiyar believes opponents are using a familiar "playbook" today to "de-legitimise" protests, but that it isn't resonating as convincingly.

Nevertheless, the youth protests have struggled to recapture this summer's momentum.

CJP leaders, including spokesperson Saurav Das, have faced repeated detentions and legal action. Das and fellow leader Ashutosh Ranka spent a week in Delhi's Tihar jail after being accused of trespassing at Jantar Mantar.

The site of their summer victory has since been struck off the list of authorised protest venues, a decision being challenged in court.

Protesters from other groups, including the left-wing All India Students' Association (Aisa), have also faced police action over allegations of defying orders.

"We were expecting some kind of crackdown," said Das. He added that "the government has learnt a lot" since the summer.

Legal experts warn the proceedings themselves can have a chilling effect.

"A lot of cases can lead to acquittals, but it can take years. The process is the punishment, and that can deter protesters," said Ali Khan, an assistant professor at Lloyd Law College.

The restrictions on demonstrations have become excessive, according to constitutional lawyer Vrinda Grover, who is advising the CJP.

"Those who are organising the protests have repeatedly emphasised that this is non-violent," she argued. "Rights have been whittled down in the name of law and order."

The BJP has rejected suggestions it is suppressing peaceful dissent.

Islam told the BBC that demonstrations "cannot override the rights of other citizens just because a handful of people want to protest and be responsible for violence".

Even dissenting online carries risk. Sakhi's viral social media posts have attracted targeted abuse and transphobic attacks. The BBC has seen posts threatening them with violence and rape.

Sometimes, it can deter Sakhi from protesting or even make them change the way they dress.

"Making people laugh can turn into being called anti-national," Sakhi said. "They want me to feel damaged," they added.

They claim some of their content was removed after getting millions of views.

Under India's information technology laws, the government can order platforms to block content on national security grounds. Notices on X and Instagram have shown accounts being withheld in India.

CJP leaders have likened the crackdown to the 1975 Emergency, when then prime minister Indira Gandhi suspended civil liberties and jailed political opponents.

Opposition parties have, in part, filled the void. Tens of thousands gathered in Delhi on 1 November for a rally organised by INDIA bloc , an alliance of opposition parties led by Congress, and permitted by the authorities.

CJP leaders, meanwhile, insist the movement is bigger than their organisation.

When Das walked out Delhi's Tihar prison on 21 October, photographs showed him smiling.

"I would just say wait and watch," Das told us. "Time is on our side. We are a very young generation."

India 'cockroach' leaders who called on election chief to quit are freed from jail

Delhi sees more protests as freed 'cockroach' group's leaders vow to fight on

Thousands of security personnel deployed as Delhi braces for ‘cockroach’ protest

items.title: Maicol suicida a 15 anni, si rafforza la pista dei bulli: presto sentiti i compagni
items.summary: Il ragazzo voleva affrontare un percorso di transizione di genere ed era seguito dall’Asl. L’ultimo post alle amiche. Al vaglio il telefono
items.content:
Aveva quindici anni, un’identità che stava cercando di affermare e una sofferenza nata tra i banchi di scuola , dove le sue scelte di vita sarebbero state derise. Maicol mercoledì pomeriggio si è tolto la vita, gettandosi dal balcone della palazzina in cui abitava, in un quartiere residenziale di Roma Nord. Adesso, dietro quella morte, c’è una domanda alla quale la procura di Roma vuole trovare una risposta: quanto possono aver pesato le parole degli altri, le prese in giro, le umiliazioni che Maicol avrebbe subito perché voleva cambiare sesso? Per questo oltre all’analisi del cellulare della vittima gli investigatori a breve ascolteranno amici, insegnanti e compagni di classe del quindicenne.

Il bullismo e la scuola . Parte da questi due elementi l’indagine del pubblico ministero Antonio Clemente . Ed è un’inchiesta complessa. Lo è perché il principale sospettato è il bullismo. E soprattutto per il contesto in cui sarebbe maturato, un istituto scolastico. L’inchiesta per istigazione al suicidio va oltre il titolo di reato ipotizzato per poter effettuare gli accertamenti di rito, per l’autopsia già delegata ai medici dell’ospedale Gemelli. Piuttosto si tratta di un lavoro costretto a entrare nella vita di un adolescente, nelle sue fragilità, nei rapporti con i coetanei e in quel mondo, la scuola, che dovrebbe essere un luogo di crescita e protezione. E che invece, secondo il racconto dei genitori della vittima, per il quindicenne sarebbe diventato anche uno spazio di sofferenza. Perché il ragazzo veniva deriso per la sua identità di genere, per la decisione di intraprendere un percorso di transizione. Scherni che, stando alle prime testimonianze, andavano avanti da tempo, fin dalle scuole medie. Le superiori sembravano aver segnato un punto di svolta, ma un litigio con una compagna di classe avrebbe complicato nuovamente le cose.

Il quindicenne, infatti, si era progressivamente isolato. Affrontava una forma di depressione che in passato lo aveva già portato a tentare di togliersi la vita. I genitori, separati ma rimasti in buoni rapporti, avevano cercato di sostenerlo. Rispettavano ogni sua scelta. Il ragazzo era anche seguito dal Centro di igiene mentale della Asl di riferimento, dove riceveva assistenza psichiatrica.

Il giorno prima del suicidio, sarebbe arrivata una delusione. Un sentimento non corrisposto di cui ha anche scritto in un messaggio lasciato in camera e sequestrato dagli inquirenti. Agli atti ci sono anche i post inviati agli amici, nei quali aveva annunciato la volontà di uccidersi. Segnali che adesso gli investigatori stanno cercando di ricostruire, per capire cosa sia accaduto nelle ore e nei giorni precedenti alla tragedia.

La procura vuole approfondire ogni aspetto, senza dare per scontato che esista un unico motivo, una sola responsabilità, un episodio capace di spiegare tutto.

Il magistrato ha già ascoltato i genitori. Il padre è italiano, la madre è originaria dell’Europa orientale. Una famiglia come tante. Sono stati loro a raccontare le difficoltà del figlio, le confidenze raccolte negli ult imi mesi, le prese in giro che avrebbe subito tra i banchi di scuola. Parole che adesso dovranno essere verificate, ascoltando chi con il quindicenne condivideva le giornate: gli amici, i compagni di classe, gli insegnanti.

Perché è lì, nella quotidianità scolastica, che gli investigatori intendono cercare risposte. Chi lo derideva? Quanto spesso accadeva? Qualcuno sapeva?

Occorrono testimonianze, riscontri, elementi concreti. Bisogna distinguere eventuali episodi di bullismo, ricostruire il contesto, non solo scolastico. Altre informazioni arriveranno dal telefono cellulare del quindicenne, sequestrato su disposizione della procura. Gli agenti del commissariato Flaminio Nuovo, ai quali sono state affidate le indagini, analizzeranno messaggi, conversazioni e contatti.

items.title: Terminal borders that don't cost a cell
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.joshka.net/cell-borders/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50491423 Points: 231 # Comments: 98
items.content:
This post (and the code behind it) was written with a lot of help from AI. I'm not going to apologize for that. If that bothers you, feel free to close the tab.

I maintain Ratatui , so I see a lot of the TUIs people build. Many of them end up looking fairly same-ish: plain boxes on a boring background, missing a bunch of the things that good design in other mediums brings us.

Borders are part of the problem. They have to take up space, so they become part of the panels people want to build. One option is to drop them and just use color, but borders are really nice for delineating and surrounding things. There are lots of ways to sort of get borders in a terminal, but none that are 100% good. I've drawn enough ┌──┐ by hand to have opinions about this.

The usual way is the Unicode Box Drawing block, which has 128 characters for lines, corners and joins. Somehow that's still not enough:

So I've been working on a terminal protocol that draws thin lines on the edges of cells instead. I've got it working as a patch to Ghostty (and an earlier version in Rio before that), and I've built demo apps for it with Ratatui. I'd like feedback from terminal and TUI authors.

Every line in that screenshot is a cell border. None of them use up a row or column. The tab labels sit on the top edge of each pane, the text fields are underlined right under the text, and the buttons are one row tall and rounded.

Here's the same app in a terminal without cell borders, falling back to box-drawing characters:

Each pane loses a row and a column on every side, so the log pane shows two fewer lines and the notes wrap differently. The tab labels move inside the frame. The text fields use the underline attribute instead, and the checkbox and buttons turn into brackets.

The settings form, with cell borders and then with the box-drawing fallback:

The tabs are the same story. With cell borders they sit on the pane's top edge. With box characters they need their own row inside the frame:

Lines between cells also work for charts. btop-style braille graphs fill every cell with dots, so there's nowhere to put a gridline or an average line without giving up a row. With cell borders they sit on the cell edges between the dots. Here's a monitor in that style, built with Ratatui:

Here's the tiling panes demo moving panes around, opening menus and the about dialog:

Partway through, it turns on a checkerboard of the cells, which shows how everything lines up with the grid. Toggle it here:

The root of it is that box-drawing characters are text. Each line is a glyph that takes up a whole cell, and pretty much everything annoying about them falls out of that.

Space is the obvious one. On my 16" laptop with a font I can actually read, the terminal is something like 200x50 (your prefs will move that around a bit). Columns are mostly fine at that size. Rows aren't. A layout with a couple of levels of nested panels can easily spend 6 or 8 of those 50 rows on nothing but lines. That's a lot of screen to give up for decoration.

You also can't put a line between two cells that both have something in them. So there's no way to underline a text field right under its text, or to outline a button, without adding padding around it. Rounded corners sort of work, except the corner glyph has one background color, and when the panel's background is different from what's around it you get a little square of the wrong color in each corner. And the line itself is whatever the font decides it is, weight and position included.

Then there's copy and paste. Select some text inside a box and you get the box too. Everyone who's pasted from a TUI into Slack knows the little │ cleanup dance. Sometimes you do want the box (pasting a table into a chat, say), but mostly it's junk. Cell borders aren't text, so they never get copied, which cuts both ways.

A cell border is a cell attribute, like a background color. Each cell can carry up to twelve line segments: the two halves of each of its four edges, and four arms from its center. Each segment has its own color, width, placement and style, and the terminal draws them over the cell grid. Borders are stored in the cells, so they scroll, erase, insert and reflow with the text. What happens on erase or scroll already has an answer, the same one as for colors.

The edges are split into halves so borders line up with quadrant block characters ( ▖▗▘▝ and friends). That makes it easy to draw a shape that's a half cell in from the grid and still put a neat border around it. Yes, that still uses a character for the fill, and there might be a better way to do that part. One problem at a time.

The same idea could stretch to sextants and octants, or to quarter and eighth widths, if designs need them.

Lines can be solid, double, dashed or dotted. Each corner and center of a cell can be square or rounded, with a configurable radius and anti-aliased arcs. A rounded corner can name an outside color, so the area outside the arc is painted correctly when the panel's background differs from what's behind it.

When two neighboring cells both put a line on their shared edge, they merge into one line. The stroke with the higher priority wins, then the wider one, then the one to the right or below. That way a focused pane can raise its priority and keep its whole outline, whatever order its neighbors were drawn in. My first try was "right/bottom always wins", which lasted until the focused pane lost half its outline to its neighbor.

The common path is a pen, held in the cursor like the current background color. Set it, print some text, and the printed cells get the borders:

There are also rectangle commands that set or clear borders on existing cells without touching the pen, and a capability query. An app sends the query followed by DA1. If the DA1 reply arrives without a cell-border reply first, the terminal doesn't support it, so the app falls back to box characters and reserves the space they need. Terminals that don't understand the DCS ignore it, the same as any unknown DCS.

The minimum a terminal needs is the pen, the rectangle commands and solid strokes. I've tried to keep that first cut small, because there's always one more "... and this" to add, and that's a slippery slope.

Line styles, rounded joints, priority and outside colors are extension fields listed in the capability reply, and unknown fields are ignored, so they can be added later. I'd rather the early decisions be two way doors where possible.

The spec calls itself version 1 (it's the 1 in DCS 1 + b ). That's v1 in the old sense, before we all got bogged down in semver. It doesn't mean done or stable, it means it's the first one I was willing to write down. Read it as v0.1, or a draft, or whatever you prefer.

What none of these give you is a line with its own color and width on each edge. The rationale document covers the prior art in more detail and explains each choice in the protocol.

My own first prototype was in Rio ( raphamorim/rio#1947 ), with an earlier version of the spec that used APC instead of DCS. Feedback pointed out that APC isn't safe to reuse: Kermit 95 has run APC payloads as Kermit commands since the 90s. DCS is where structured terminal commands already live, and terminals ignore DCS strings they don't recognize, so I switched to that.

When I first showed this around, most of the questions were about these. The spec goes into all of them properly, but here's roughly where I landed.

Multiplexers were the first thing people asked about. tmux and friends redraw panes from their own idea of the cell grid, so passing these sequences through would just put borders in the wrong place. A multiplexer that doesn't know about the protocol should drop them and answer DA1 itself, and then apps running inside it fall back to box characters like they would anywhere else. One that does know about it can store borders like any other attribute and redraw them.

Conflicting lines on a shared edge are settled when the terminal renders, using the priority rule above, so it doesn't matter what order the app wrote the cells in.

Erase, insert and delete all work the way they do for background colors. Erased cells pick up the current pen, and lines that get inserted or deleted take their borders along. Scrollback, the alternate screen and reflow mostly come for free, because the border lives in the cell.

On cost: the Ghostty change is about 1,650 lines, and a fair chunk of that is tests. Each cell gets a 16-bit border ID, which fits in padding that was already there, so cells don't get any bigger and a screen with no borders costs nothing extra. The IDs point into a table of distinct border sets (about 100 bytes each) that's shared by the whole terminal. A typical TUI only uses a handful of distinct sets, but the table is never freed, so in the worst case (all 65,535 IDs in use) it's somewhere around 10-15 MB.

Rendering only does extra work for cells that have borders. Each one looks at its four neighbors to resolve shared edges, so changing a row also rebuilds the rows either side of it. Straight lines are a few solid quads per cell. Rounded corners cost more, because the anti-aliased arc is drawn as rows of small quads, roughly one per edge pixel. I haven't benchmarked any of this properly yet, and it's the part I'd most like another set of eyes on.

items.title: How Not to Build a Music Player
items.summary: Article URL: https://alichraghi.github.io/blog/how-not-to-build-a-music-player/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50491400 Points: 105 # Comments: 40
items.content:
The Twelve-Day War made me realize online music players aren’t a viable option for those who live under an oppressive regime that disconnects the internet across the country as a way to silence public opinion.

So, as soon as the connection came back, I started archiving tracks and looking for offline alternatives and discovered Strawberry . It’s a feature-rich music player and kept me happy for quite a while, but I have this habit of looking at song lyrics and singing along! Strawberry fetches lyrics from the internet when it recognizes a song, but sometimes the lyrics weren’t line-synced and worse, it displayed the timestamps next to the lyrics which I found pretty annoying to look at. I wasn’t aware of other music players such as foobar2000 which my friend just pointed me to while writing this post.

I decided to write my own music player and call it AMP with a few goals in mind: minimal feature-set, no C++ dependencies, proper system integration to make it feel like a native app, and of course, write it in Zig (including the shaders!). I also wanted to roll my own UI because of the fun memories of working on V’s UI during my first days of being introduced into system programming. But before I could make any meaningful progress, a new wave of protests started. Following the tragedy of January 8 and 9 , another internet blackout began, lasting more than four months.

During the blackout, there were these anonymous people on Telegram selling internet access through personal White SIMs , whitelisted servers, Starlink dishes, etc. A black market had formed for the freaking internet! You’d get charged $5 or more for just 1GB of traffic. The prices dropped slightly after a while, but it was still hella expensive. The regime surely made a lot of money out of it. I ended up spending hundreds of dollars on these services and other methods just to stay in touch with my friends and keep my hobbies alive. Killing time was becoming a problem. Especially for someone like me who built their entire social life online.

I carefully used this slow connection to download repositories, documention, etc. to continue working on my music player. It really brought me immense joy during this hard time.

Once the connection was mostly restored to the pre-blackout days (UDP traffic is still blocked, though, which naturally also affects QUIC), my attention was shifted towards LLMs. It had become very hard for me to ignore the hype and progress around frontier LLMs. As I really never thought about using them seriously for coding. They are still everywhere in the news, and I was just reminded that I owned a Claude Max 20x subscription gift from my boss back in 2025. Eating dust and maybe soon expiring. So I decided to give it a try and experiment on my music player. It was a very addictive experience. I literally couldn’t hit the plan limits no matter how hard I tried, so after a few non-stop days of prompting, a good chunk of AMP was vibecoded..

At the time, I thought this was an okay approach for a hobby project and I could just un-slopify it later. Little did I know I’m mentally incapable of reviewing tens of thousands lines of code. Shortly after, Anthropic figured that I live in Iran and instantly banned my account. Then Codeberg announced its no-AI policy , which gave me two choices. Either get rid of all that slop or move the repository elsewhere. Going with the former option, I started reading every single line of code, rewriting them. I was surprised by my own ignorance and how much LLMs like to complicate stuff. (I wish I could show an example, but my memory is extremely fragile and I’ve got no pre-rewrite history of the repo to check).

Four months later, nearly half the codebase is gone, and somehow it’s more robust with the same set of features (and more). I regret relying on LLMs in the first place, but hey, lesson learned. That said I think it’s still possible to create a healthy relationship with LLMs as long as you look at them as a fancy IDE feature. A lot of times they are just running long sed or regex commands that are a no-brainer act for humans when done by hand but still consumes a good time. For now and hopefully forever I think I’ll be going the old school way. Never rush your hobbies!

Worth mentioning that the blur shader is written in Zig based on this excellent blog post! .

items.title: How the Jensen Huang scandal created a headache for business-friendly Singapore
items.summary: The scandal has cast a spotlight on Singapore's success as a chip hub - and a location for alleged illicit trade.
items.content:
A major scandal involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy based in Singapore has cast a spotlight on the city-state's success as a global chip hub - and a location for alleged illicit trade.

On Thursday, Huang stepped down from the US chip giant after admitting he had an affair. He was reportedly involved with a woman named Alice Huang, who ran Singaporean data centre company Megaspeed, a major buyer of Nvidia's chips.

For decades, Singapore has painstakingly cultivated a reputation as an open, business-friendly economy offering easy access to both the US and Chinese markets.

With the AI boom, it has become a major hub for the trade of high-end semiconductor chips in recent years.

Singapore was the second-largest billing centre globally last year for Nvidia, accounting for nearly a fifth of what the US chip giant earns.

But notably, less than 1% of its earnings were for chips that actually entered Singapore, as the island acts as a hub for many Asian companies to place orders and send them elsewhere.

Since 2022, when the US restricted advanced American semiconductors from being exported to China or acquired by Chinese companies, US officials have been concerned that other countries such as Singapore could be used by Chinese companies to gain access to the chips.

It became the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia and is suspected of giving backdoor access to these chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.

Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations.

It has charged four companies and five individuals - including Chinese nationals - for various offences including fraud, following US concerns that Chinese AI company DeepSeek had been buying Nvidia chips from third parties in Singapore, among other places.

They also tried to probe Megaspeed, but were faced with a number of difficulties.

In a statement released on Thursday, the government said that since February 2025, they had been looking into whether Megaspeed and other firms had made false declarations about data servers which were purchased and exported through Singapore.

The companies stated the equipment would end up in neighbouring Malaysia, but Singapore authorities suspect the equipment's final destinations were elsewhere.

Singapore said it sought assistance from US authorities several times to get more information from one of the investigated companies - Supermicro, a US-based company which the BBC understands was supplying computer servers to Megaspeed.

But "despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance", it said in its statement. The BBC has sought comment from the US State Department.

Singapore authorities said they had also investigated Alice Huang - not for espionage, but for any possible role in Megaspeed's suspected fraud.

In the end, they found "insufficient evidence" of crime and let her leave Singapore in February this year, after holding her passport for several months.

Since launching their probe nearly two years ago, Singapore has yet to bring any charges against Megaspeed or any of the companies and individuals linked to the case.

Singapore and US investigations into Megaspeed are still ongoing.

In 2024, US officials had paid a visit to a Malaysian data centre owned by Megaspeed and saw Nvidia technology still in their boxes, raising concerns that Megaspeed was shipping high-end chips out elsewhere, according to a report by the New York Times.

Last year, Megaspeed appeared to have imported 50,000 more chips than Nvidia could account for, according to a Bloomberg report. Nvidia later adjusted its own figures after visiting more warehouses.

Megaspeed has maintained it has always acted lawfully and that previous inspections by authorities found no evidence of illegal activity.

On Thursday, the company said it "welcomes appropriate government scrutiny" and that it is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government".

China has also long refuted accusations that its companies and institutions are illegally obtaining high-end US chips.

How Megaspeed and Alice Huang came to Singapore highlights other vulnerabilities stemming from the city-state's openness.

In recent years, the city-state has become a prime destination for Chinese companies, with tech firms such as TikTok and Manus making it their global headquarters. Besides Singapore's ease of doing business, it has a population that is mostly ethnically Chinese and largely views China positively.

For a Chinese firm, Singapore offers a base near the mainland and a "neutral address" that global customers and investors accept, said Winston Ma, adjunct professor at New York University's School of Law.

But critics say this has given rise to "Singapore-washing", where Chinese companies use the city-state's clean image to obscure their origins, reduce suspicions and even cover up dubious activities.

Washington-based security analysis group C4ADS told the BBC they had assessed Alice Huang's setup of Megaspeed to be such a case.

BBC checks of corporate records in China, Hong Kong and Singapore found that in 2019, Huang sold a gaming company and its subsidiaries to Chinese gaming firm 7Road.

In March 2023, a 7Road subsidiary in Singapore named Huang as its executive director. The next day it changed its name - to Megaspeed.

Huang was in charge for eight months before she transferred the company to a Singaporean man.

During this period, Megaspeed went through "a critical period of corporate restructuring and regional expansion", and her corporate relationships raised questions about whether "Megaspeed's Singaporean identity is genuine or effectively Chinese-controlled", according to C4ADS.

Even after she transferred Megaspeed, C4ADS assessed that she was still "practically in control" of the company, based on her links to Megaspeed via another company as well as LinkedIn posts where she continued to identify herself as Megaspeed's "chairwoman" at conferences.

Megaspeed has not answered BBC queries regarding the company's and Alice Huang's links to China and the Chinese government.

"For the longest time, Singapore has managed to enjoy the best of both worlds with excellent relations with US and China," Nanyang Technological University politics and international studies lecturer Dylan Loh said.

Singapore has long positioned itself as a neutral party between the two superpowers. Its prime minister Lawrence Wong has insisted that his country is neither pro-China nor pro-America, but "pro-Singapore".

But Loh says this balancing act "has now fast become very difficult to manage and sometimes quite fraught too" with the US-China dispute over chips.

With the Megaspeed case, the tightrope Singapore has walked is set to get even narrower, according to analysts.

Beijing may ask why Singapore is investigating issues pertaining to US restrictions and whether they are siding with the US' interests, says Chong Ja Ian, a Singaporean political scientist and non-resident scholar with Carnegie China.

Washington, in turn, might read Singapore's latest statement as "pushing blame" on the US, which could lead to backlash from the White House, he said.

"Singapore has made a policy position not to take sides. But by not choosing a side, they run the risk of being seen as complicit" in either side's agenda, he said.

But Benjamin Ho, an assistant professor and China expert at Singapore's S Rajaratnam School of International Studies, noted that this was "not the first or last time Singapore will be caught between the US and China".

"This is the price that an open economy has to grapple with - you get caught in the middle when things turn sour."

Additional reporting by Jack Lau of the BBC's Global China Unit.

The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal

How could the Nvidia CEO’s affair threaten US national security?

How AI visionary Jensen Huang was undone by his own bad decisions

items.title: S&P conferma il rating sull'Italia: 'La crescita supererà le stime'. Giorgetti: 'È la strada giusta'
items.summary: Il ministro dell'Economia: 'Bene, in tempi difficili è un successo'
items.content:
Standard and Poor's conferma i rating sull'Italia di "BBB+/A-2", con outlook positivo, apprezzando l'impegno sui conti e sulla stabilizzazione del debito . Valuta inoltre che la crescita economica dell'Italia supererà le stime precedenti, trainata da un contesto esterno favorevole per le esportazioni nette (esclusa l'energia) e dal perdurare degli stimoli legati al programma Ngeu" mentre "per il periodo 2027-2029, la crescita dovrebbe mantenersi su livelli modesti ma stabili".

"E' un'ulteriore conferma che siamo sulla strada giusta - commenta a caldo il ministro dell'Economia, Giancarlo Giorgetti - In tempi così difficili una conferma rappresenta un successo". Il rating di S&P arriva al termine di una giornata che ha visto diffondere i dati dell'andamento del Pil in Europa nel terzo trimestre, che vede l'Ue crescere dello 0,5%, quello dell'Eurozona dello 0,4% e l'Italia ferma. Sui prossimi mesi si allunga poi l'ombra del caro energia: a settembre i prezzi delle importazioni italiane sono balzati del 9,6% su base annua. Per ora l'Italia non passa in serie A, ma la decisione di un rialzo non era semplice nell'attuale contesto.

A gennaio l'agenzia aveva posto due condizioni per un nuovo rialzo : che il Paese rafforzasse la propria solidità finanziaria verso l'estero ("Prevediamo che il debito estero netto dell'Italia scenda al di sotto del 150% delle entrate delle partite correnti entro il 2028", scrive oggi) e che riducesse il deficit in modo da far scendere il rapporto del debito sul Pil. Anche i mercati non sembrano vedere grandi novità : lo spread tra Btp e Bund tedeschi a 10 anni ha chiuso a 104 punti, invariato rispetto alla vigilia, mentre il rendimento dei decennali italiani è rimasto al 4,41%, fotografando un costo del debito italiano ancora elevato. Sul fronte dei prezzi, l'Istat ha registrato a settembre un rincaro delle importazioni dell'1,9% in un mese, trainato soprattutto dall'energia. Il deficit energetico italiano è salito a 5,9 miliardi, da 3,8 miliardi un anno prima , anche se la bilancia commerciale complessiva resta in attivo per 2,1 miliardi.

L'export aumenta del 3,8% in valore ma cala del 3,4% in volume. Il problema è europeo: a settembre la bilancia commerciale Ue è passata dall'avanzo di 11,4 miliardi di un anno prima a un deficit di 16,8 miliardi. Il disavanzo energetico è aumentato da 24,1 a 37,6 miliardi. Nei primi nove mesi dell'anno gli scambi con l'estero dell'Unione hanno accumulato un passivo di 83,2 miliardi, contro un attivo di 85,5 miliardi nel 2025. Intanto cresce l'attesa per le nuove previsioni economiche che presenterà martedì 17 novembre la Commissione europea. Il commissario all'Economia Valdis Dombrovskis ha già anticipato giovedì che con ogni probabilità saranno riviste al rialzo sia le stime sulla crescita sia quelle sull'inflazione.

A maggio Bruxelles prevedeva per quest'anno un Pil in aumento dell'1,1% nell'Ue e dello 0,9% nell'Eurozona. Ora avverte che i rincari, spinti dall'energia, potrebbero durare più a lungo e trasmettersi al resto dell'economia. I dati Eurostat sul Pil mostrano intanto un'Europa a più velocità: nel terzo trimestre , ad esempio, la Germania è cresciuta dello 0,2%, la Spagna dello 0,6%, mentre la Francia ha segnato -0,1%. Per l'Italia il responso è di uno zero per cento tondo, dopo il +0,2% dei tre mesi precedenti. Su base annua la crescita italiana è dello 0,8%, contro l'1,3% dell'Eurozona e l'1,5% dell'Ue.
